title: Culture: What You Do Is Who You Are
author: Samuel Crome
summary: Prompted by reading Ben Horowitz's What You Do Is Who You Are, a school leader uses the culture of the samurai -- Bushido, Shugyo (daily pursuit of mastery), and Giri (mutual accountability) -- as an extended analogy for school culture, arguing that identity and mission are lived through consistent action rather than declared through aspirational language. The piece's central claim, borrowed directly from Horowitz, is that most organisations' stated values ('integrity,' 'equality') are aspirational and largely ignored, while 'virtues' -- concrete, trackable, habitual behaviours -- actually shape how decisions get made when leaders aren't watching. The author extends this to schools, warning against "Mission Creep," where leaders assume a culture is in place that staff cannot actually articulate, and offers practical diagnostics such as asking new staff what the culture genuinely feels like rather than relying on leaders' own self-assessment. The piece closes by insisting culture is never finished -- it requires constant attention to small details (like uniform slippage) and ongoing willingness to add to or evolve virtues as a school changes.
points: The central argument, drawn from Ben Horowitz, is that culture is defined by how an organisation actually resolves problems and makes decisions day to day -- not by the values staff can recite from a handbook.

Horowitz's distinction between values (aspirational, often ignored) and virtues (concrete, trackable, habitual behaviours) gives school leaders a practical mechanism for closing the gap between stated mission and lived experience.
The piece names "Mission Creep" as a specific failure mode: leaders assume a culture is embedded when, upon evaluation, staff cannot actually identify which values or behaviours matter.

A leader's own perception of culture is explicitly unreliable; the recommended diagnostic is asking new staff what the culture feels like after a few weeks, since they experience the unstated social norms most acutely.
Culture maintenance is framed as perpetual and detail-level work (noticing an untucked shirt, tracking whether small norms are slipping) rather than a project that is ever finished.
quotes: 'Your culture is how your organisation makes decisions when you're not there. It's how they resolve problems every day. If you don't methodically set your culture, then two thirds of it will end up being accidental and it will be a mistake' Ben Horowitz

He suggests that we adopt virtues instead, which, like the Samurai's focus on actions, ensure that we will actually do things that we believe in. These must be operational, concrete, and create habitual behaviours.

Often called Mission Creep, sometimes leaders assume a certain culture is in place, but, when it is evaluated, it turns out that many in the organisation don't actually know which values or actions are important. Lack of clarity is a culture killer.

'Your own perspective on the culture is not that relevant; this is rarely what your staff will experience. The real question is - what must employees do to survive and succeed in your organisation? Which behaviours get them included, or excluded from things? What gets them ahead?'

My job as a leader is to constantly question and consider these things, so that cultural norms become embedded and the easiest way to behave. Clarity and consistency are important here, so nothing can be left to chance.

A perfect culture is unattainable. We have never finished. Every day things can disrupt the culture you seek to build, so we have to keep defining our virtues and then walking the walk - both stating and modelling them.
